grammar.title: Countable and uncountable nouns; determiners
points: Countable nouns have a singular and a plural form: one ticket, three tickets. Some plurals are irregular: man - men, foot - feet.
Uncountable nouns have no plural and take a singular verb: The furniture is new. To count them, use a phrase: a piece of advice, two bottles of water.
Use some in positive sentences and any in negatives and most questions: We need some rice. There isn't any sugar. Use some in offers: Would you like some juice?
No + noun means 'not any' and goes with a positive verb: There are no buses today.
Use many with plural countable nouns and much with uncountable nouns, mostly in negatives and questions: How many eggs? Not much time.
A lot of and plenty of work with both types; several goes only with plural countable nouns: several shops.

grammar.title: -ing forms
points: Add -ing to the verb: read - reading. Watch the spelling: make - making, swim - swimming.
Use the -ing form after verbs of liking and disliking: enjoy, love, like, hate, don't mind, can't stand. Example: I can't stand waiting for buses.
Use the -ing form after adjective + preposition: good at, bad at, keen on, interested in, afraid of, tired of. Example: Marta is keen on skating.
An -ing form can be the subject of a sentence: Cycling to school keeps me fit.

grammar.title: Present simple and continuous
points: Present simple: add -s or -es for he, she, it (she plays, he watches). Use do/does for questions and don't/doesn't for negatives.
Use the present simple for habits, routines and facts: The shop opens at nine. Water freezes at zero degrees.
Present continuous = am/is/are + -ing. Use it for actions happening now or around now: Be quiet, the baby is sleeping.
Use the present continuous for fixed future arrangements: We're meeting Tom on Friday.
State verbs (know, like, want, believe, understand, prefer) are not normally used in the continuous: I know the answer (not I'm knowing).

grammar.title: Past simple; used to
points: Regular verbs add -ed in the past simple: walk - walked, stop - stopped, carry - carried. Many common verbs are irregular: go - went, see - saw.
Negatives and questions use did/didn't + infinitive: I didn't see him. Did you call her? The verb be uses was/were and no did.
Use the past simple for finished actions, often with a time: We moved here in 2019.
Used to + infinitive describes past habits or situations that are not true now: I used to have long hair.
Negative and question forms drop the -d: I didn't use to like fish. Did you use to play outside?

grammar.title: Modals: obligation, necessity and advice (1)
points: Must, should and ought to never change form and are followed by the infinitive: You must stop. He should rest. We ought to leave.
Have to changes like a normal verb: she has to, do you have to?, he doesn't have to.
Must and have to mean it is necessary: I have to wear a uniform. You must see a doctor.
Mustn't means it is forbidden or very important not to do it. Don't have to means it is not necessary: You mustn't touch that. You don't have to pay.
Should and ought to give advice (a good idea); shouldn't means a bad idea. They are weaker than must: You should drink more water.

grammar.title: Present perfect and past simple
points: Present perfect = have/has + past participle: I've finished. She hasn't called. Have you eaten?
Use the past simple for finished actions at a finished time (yesterday, last year, in 2020): I lost my keys on Monday.
Use the present perfect when the time is not said, or when the result matters now: I've lost my keys (I still can't find them).
Just (a moment ago) and already (sooner than expected) go between have and the participle: He's just left. I've already seen it.
Yet goes at the end of negatives and questions: I haven't started yet. Ever (at any time) is used in questions: Have you ever ridden a horse?

grammar.title: Comparative and superlative adjectives
points: Short adjectives add -er / -est: tall - taller - the tallest. Note the spelling: large - larger, hot - hotter, easy - easier.
Longer adjectives use more / the most: more expensive, the most expensive.
Irregular forms: good - better - the best; bad - worse - the worst; far - further - the furthest.
Compare two things with a comparative + than: Trains are faster than buses. Use less + adjective + than for the opposite: The film is less exciting than the book.
As + adjective + as means the two are equal; not as ... as means less: I'm as tall as my mum. Tea isn't as strong as coffee.
Use the + superlative (or the least + adjective) to compare one with all the others: It's the oldest house in the village.

grammar.title: Future forms; future continuous
points: Present continuous + a time = fixed arrangements: I'm seeing the dentist at four.
Will + infinitive is for predictions, offers and promises: I think robots will do more jobs. I'll carry that for you.
Be going to + infinitive is for plans and intentions you already have: We're going to paint my room this weekend.
Future continuous = will/won't be + -ing: I'll be travelling. Will you be using the car?
Use the future continuous for an action that will be in progress at a certain time in the future: This time tomorrow I'll be sitting on the beach.

grammar.title: Conditional sentences
points: Zero conditional: if + present, present. Use it for things that are always true: If you heat ice, it melts. Here if can mean when.
First conditional: if + present, will/won't + infinitive. Use it for real possibilities in the future: If it rains, we'll stay at home.
Second conditional: if + past simple, would/wouldn't + infinitive. Use it for unreal or unlikely situations: If I had a boat, I would sail to Ibiza.
The if-clause can come first (with a comma) or second (no comma): We'll miss the bus if we don't hurry.
Unless means 'if ... not': I won't go unless you come too (= if you don't come).

grammar.title: Past perfect
points: Past perfect = had + past participle, the same for all persons: I had left. She hadn't eaten. Had they arrived?
Use it for an action that happened before another action or time in the past: When we got to the station, the train had gone.
The later action is in the past simple; the earlier one is in the past perfect: I was hungry because I hadn't had breakfast.
It often appears with already, just, never, after, before and by the time: By the time Dad came home, we had already cooked dinner.

grammar.title: Modals: obligation, necessity and advice (2)
points: Should / shouldn't + infinitive gives advice: You should pack a jumper. You shouldn't carry too much cash.
Need to + infinitive means it is important or necessary: You need to book early in summer.
Have to + infinitive means it is necessary because of a rule or law: You have to wear a seat belt.
When something is not necessary, use don't have to, don't need to or needn't: You don't have to come. You don't need to hurry.
Needn't is followed by the infinitive without to: You needn't bring food (not needn't to bring).

grammar.title: The passive
points: Passive = the verb be + past participle. Change be to show the tense.
Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle: These phones are made in Korea.
Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: The bridge was built in 1890.
With modal verbs use modal + be + past participle: Helmets must be worn. It can be done.
Use the passive when we don't know or don't care who does the action, or to focus on the thing affected.
Add by + agent if you need to say who did it: The song was written by a teenager.

grammar.title: Relative clauses
points: Defining relative clauses say which person or thing we mean. They have no commas: The boy who sits next to me is Italian.
Use who for people, which for things, that for people or things, whose for possession and where for places.
In defining clauses you can leave out who, which or that when it is the object: The film (that) we saw was great. You cannot leave it out when it is the subject.
Non-defining relative clauses add extra information and go between commas: My aunt, who lives in Vigo, is a chef.
In non-defining clauses you cannot use that and you can never leave out the pronoun.

grammar.title: Articles: a/an, the and zero article
points: Use a/an with a singular countable noun when you mention it for the first time or say someone's job: I saw a fox. She's an engineer.
Use the when you mention something again, when there is only one, or when it is clear which one you mean: The fox ran away. The moon is bright.
Use the with superlatives and with seas, rivers, mountain ranges and plural country names: the best, the Atlantic, the Alps, the Netherlands.
Use no article (zero article) for plural or uncountable nouns in general: Cats love fish. Music helps me relax.
Use no article with most countries, cities, streets, languages, meals and phrases like at home, at school, by bus.

grammar.title: Reported speech
points: When the reporting verb is past (said, told), the tense usually moves back: present simple to past simple, present continuous to past continuous, past simple and present perfect to past perfect, will to would, can to could.
Could, would, should and might do not change.
Pronouns and possessives often change: 'I like my job' - She said she liked her job.
Tell needs a person as object; say does not: He told me (that) he was tired. He said (that) he was tired.
Other reporting verbs: explain, announce, insist, demand, suggest. After insist, suggest and demand use that + clause: She suggested that we (should) leave early.
questions: 'I'm hungry.' He said he ____ hungry. | was
'I work in a bank.' She said she ____ in a bank. | worked
She ____ me that she was busy. (said / told) | told

grammar.title: Reported questions
points: Reported questions use statement word order (subject before verb) and no question mark: 'Where is the bank?' - He asked where the bank was.
Tenses move back as in reported statements: 'What are you doing?' - She asked what I was doing.
Do, does and did disappear: 'Where do you live?' - She asked where I lived.
For yes/no questions use if or whether: 'Are you ready?' - She asked if I was ready.
Pronouns change to fit the speaker: 'Is this your bag?' - He asked whether it was my bag.
questions: 'Where do you live?' She asked me where I ____. | lived
'Are you tired?' He asked ____ I was tired. (if / that / what) | if

grammar.title: have something done
points: Form: have + object + past participle: I have my eyes tested every year.
Use it when another person, usually a professional, does a job for you: We had the car repaired (= a mechanic repaired it).
Compare: I cut my hair (I did it myself) and I had my hair cut (someone else did it).
Have can be in any tense, or after modals and going to: She's having her room painted. You should have that tooth checked. We're going to have a pool built.

grammar.title: Different types of clause
points: Contrast: although, whereas and while join two ideas that are different or surprising: Although it was cold, we swam. I love football, whereas my sister prefers tennis.
Although and whereas can go at the start or in the middle; while (for contrast) usually starts the sentence: While I like the city, I wouldn't live there.
Purpose: in order to + infinitive; so that + subject + verb (often can/could): I got up early in order to catch the bus. I saved money so that I could buy a bike.
Reason: because and as mean the same: We stayed in as it was raining. They can go in the middle or at the start of the sentence.
When the clause comes first, put a comma after it: As I was tired, I went to bed.

grammar.title: Verbs with two objects
points: Some verbs can have two objects: a direct object (usually a thing) and an indirect object (usually a person): Dad gave me a watch.
Pattern 1: verb + person + thing, with no preposition: She sent her friend a postcard.
Pattern 2: verb + thing + to/for + person: She sent a postcard to her friend.
Use to with give, send, show, lend, tell, teach, offer, pay, bring and write. Use for with buy, make, get, cook, find and save.
When the thing is a pronoun (it, them), use pattern 2: I gave it to Leo (not I gave Leo it).
questions: I lent my bike ____ Pablo. (to / for) | to
Mum made a cake ____ me. (to / for) | for

Rewrite without 'to': He sent a text to Ana. | He sent Ana a text.
